The continuum hypothesis has a determinate truth value, though I'd frame it carefully. CH is a well-defined statement in the language of set theory—"there is no set whose cardinality is strictly between that of the integers and the reals"—so it expresses a definite proposition about the cumulative hierarchy. The independence results (Gödel's consistency proof and Cohen's forcing construction) show that CH is neither provable nor refutable from ZFC, but that's a fact about formal provability, not about truth. It's analogous to how the parallel postulate is independent of the other Euclidean axioms yet still has a determinate truth value relative to a fixed interpretation of the terms.

The natural reading is that CH is either true or false in the intended universe of sets, V. What's genuinely open is which. Some set theorists (notably those working with large cardinal axioms, inner model theory, and forcing axioms like Martin's Maximum) argue that CH is actually *false*—that the "true" universe satisfies 2^ℵ₀ = ℵ₂ or similar. Others, following Gödel, suspect CH might be true in a canonical inner model. Either way, the question is substantive, not a matter of convention.

Where I'd add nuance: "determinate" can mean different things. If you mean "has a truth value in the intended model of set theory," then yes. If you mean "we have a principled way to discover it," that's much less clear, and the multiverse view (Hamkins) challenges whether there's a single intended V at all. But on the standard Platonist reading you're describing, (B) is right.
